newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Daimler first half profit more than doubles.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Daimler first half profit more than doubles.

text.p: German industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG said on Thursday its operating profit more than doubled in the first half of 1997 to 1.849 billion marks from 827 million.

The group, Germany's largest, said rising car sales, the weak mark and strict internal cost control were behind the improved performance. It also predicted that its full-year performance would be significantly better than in 1996.
Group sales were up 14 percent in the first six months to 55.9 billion marks and Daimler said full-year sales would exceed 115 billion marks, up from 106.4 billion in 1996.

Net profit rose to 1.92 billion marks from 1.52 billion. The company's share price, considered by analysts to be very well valued, slipped 4.50 marks to 154.80 as some had hoped for an operating figure of two billion marks.

"The programmes to increase efficiency have continued to improve operating results," chief executive officer Juergen Schrempp told a news conference. "Though we are not yet satisfied with the overall level of profitability, we are beginning to achieve the sort of returns we want."

Daimler's sales of its Mercedes-Benz cars rose six percent to 335,794 and Daimler said it hoped to build and sell over 700,000 in the full year. Sales of commercial vehicles rose 14 percent to 191,994.

The automotive division made an operating profit of 1.429 billion marks, up only slightly from 1.409 billion in the first half of 1996 due to high costs related to the launch of new models such as the small A-Class car and U.S.-built M-Class sports utility vehicle.

All the profit came from the car division with commercial vehicles making a small, unspecified loss. But Schrempp said he expected the commercial vehicles to make a profit this year for the first time in several years.

Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (Dasa), for years a huge drag on group earnings, finally swung back into the black, turning in an operating profit of 74 million marks, compared to a loss of 677 million marks in the first six months of 1996.

It particularly benefited from the strong dollar in which its aircraft sales are denominated. Huge losses at Dasa related to its disposal of Dutch aircraft maker Fokker forced the group to a seven billion mark loss in 1995, the largest in German corporate history.
Debis and Daimler's rail and electronics businesses were also in profit.

Chief financial officer Manfred Gentz said the group would continue to make "significant advances" during the rest of the year while Schrempp hinted that if full-year profit rose, the company would be able to up its dividend from the 1.1 marks per share it paid for 1996.
